canonicalName: Large deviations theory for Markov processes (Donsker-Varadhan, Freidlin-Wentzell)

evidence.claim: Varadhan published a general asymptotic (Laplace-type) principle relating probabilities of rare events to variational problems.
evidence.source: Crossref: Varadhan, Asymptotic probabilities and differential equations, CPAM 19 (1966)

evidence.claim: zbMATH indexes the same paper as Zbl 0147.15503, year 1966.

conceptual.note: Earliest public general statement I could evidence of the variational large-deviation principle for diffusion/Markov settings. Not the first rare-event estimate: Cramer 1938 (iid sums; zbMATH JFM 64.0529.01) and Sanov (1957, i.i.d. empirical measures) came earlier, and Venttsel-Freidlin 1970 (Russian Math. Surveys) gave the small-noise version. I did not verify the text of the 1966 paper for the statistical-mechanics free-energy modelling; that link is asserted by the catalogue summary, not evidenced here.

evidence.claim: Donsker and Varadhan, Asymptotic evaluation of certain Markov process expectations for large time, I (CPAM 28).
Same series applied to the Wiener sausage (volume of a Brownian neighbourhood), a problem of the kind arising in statistical mechanics.
evidence.source: Crossref: Asymptotics for the Wiener sausage, CPAM 28 (1975)

evidence.claim: Part IV and the polaron paper apply the variational large-deviation machinery to the polaron free energy.
evidence.source: Crossref: Asymptotics for the polaron, CPAM 36 (1983)

methodological.note: Purposeful use on target problems (Markov expectations, Wiener sausage, later polaron) starts with the 1975 series. Series parts II-IV: 1975, 1976, 1983.

evidence.claim: Title naming large deviations for Markov processes: Donsker-Varadhan, On some problems of large deviations for Markov processes (Zbl 0351.60036, 1975).
Lecture Notes in Mathematics volume title with large deviations for Markov processes, 1975.
Varadhan, Large Deviations and Applications, SIAM CBMS-NSF monograph (1984), first dedicated monograph found.

institutional.note: Earliest indexed titles (zbMATH, Crossref) naming large deviations for Markov processes are Donsker-Varadhan 1975; the generic phrase "large deviations" appears in titles from 1956 (zbMATH). Monograph names: Freidlin-Wentzell (Russian 1979; English 1984 chapters in Crossref), Varadhan 1984, Ellis 1985, Dembo-Zeitouni 1998. Search was not exhaustive; no ICM section or MSC code checked.

firstTermUse.source: https://zbmath.org/?q=an:0073.12503 (Weingarten, On the probability of large deviations for sums of bounded chance variables, zbMATH 1956; earliest indexed title found in zbMATH ti:large deviations 1930-1956)

works.citation: Cramer, Sur un nouveau theoreme-limite de la theorie des probabilites (1938), Actualites Sci. Ind. 736
works.whyItMatters: Earliest exponential large-deviation theorem for sums; classical ancestor, not Markov-process theory.

works.citation: Varadhan, Asymptotic probabilities and differential equations, CPAM 19
works.whyItMatters: General variational principle for rare events.

works.citation: Varadhan, Large Deviations and Applications, SIAM
works.whyItMatters: First systematic monograph.

works.citation: Donsker and Varadhan, Asymptotic evaluation of certain Markov process expectations for large time I
works.whyItMatters: Core variational theory for Markov process occupation measures.

works.citation: Venttsel and Freidlin, On small random perturbations of dynamical systems, Russian Math. Surveys 25
works.whyItMatters: Parallel large-deviation theory for small-noise diffusions.

works.citation: Freidlin and Wentzell, Random Perturbations of Dynamical Systems (book, chapters in Crossref)
works.whyItMatters: Systematised sample-path large deviations; 1984 is the English edition year in Crossref.

notes: Priority/ambiguity: two parallel schools (Donsker-Varadhan in the US; Venttsel-Freidlin in the USSR, 1970) and iid precursors (Cramer 1938, Sanov 1957). The statistical-mechanics origin claimed in the summary (free-energy style variational formula; Lanford 1973 entropy lecture notes, Crossref 10.1007/bfb0112756, no year in record) was not evidenced from fetched texts. zbMATH Sanov entry 1961 is "On the probability of large deviations of random variables" (Zbl 0112.10106).

evidence.claim: Yao, Theory and application of trapdoor functions, FOCS 1982: unpredictability / computational hardness yields pseudorandom sequences.
Blum and Micali, How to generate cryptographically strong sequences of pseudo random bits, FOCS 1982 (SICOMP 1984).

conceptual.note: The principle "hardness implies pseudorandomness" appears in 1982 (cryptographic, assumption: one-way/hard functions). The specific design-based generator from a function hard for small circuits, which the summary describes, is Nisan-Wigderson 1988 (see methodological). Choose 1982 if the idea is the general principle, 1988 if the combinatorial-design form. I did not read the 1982 texts to check content, only that the records exist and match titles.

evidence.claim: Nisan and Wigderson, Hardness vs. randomness, FOCS 1988: generator built from combinatorial designs and a hard function, used to derandomise BPP-type classes.
Journal version, JCSS 49 (1994).
Journal version indexed as Zbl 0821.68057.

methodological.note: First purposeful use of the tool on derandomisation. Uniform-hardness P=BPP style conclusions: Impagliazzo-Wigderson 1997 (STOC, 10.1145/258533.258590). Converse (derandomisation implies lower bounds): Kabanets-Impagliazzo 2003 (10.1145/780542.780595).

evidence.claim: Paper titled Hardness vs. randomness (FOCS 1988); survey of the same name 1989 (Structure in Complexity Theory).
Survey Hardness vs. randomness - a survey, 1989 (date not given in Crossref record).
Textbook coverage: Arora-Barak, Computational Complexity (2009); Vadhan, Pseudorandomness (2012).

institutional.note: Earliest title naming the field is the 1988 FOCS paper; zbMATH has only the 1994 journal version for 1980-1995.

works.citation: Yao, Theory and application of trapdoor functions, FOCS
works.whyItMatters: Computational-indistinguishability notion of pseudorandomness.

works.whyItMatters: Generator from a hard problem; start of the hardness-to-randomness line.

works.whyItMatters: Design-based generator; names the programme.

works.whyItMatters: Journal version.

works.whyItMatters: Derandomisation of BPP from worst-case hardness.

works.whyItMatters: Sharpened hardness-randomness tradeoff.

works.citation: Kabanets and Impagliazzo, Derandomizing polynomial identity tests means proving circuit lower bounds, STOC
works.whyItMatters: Converse direction linking derandomisation to lower bounds.

works.citation: Vadhan, Pseudorandomness, Foundations and Trends in TCS
works.whyItMatters: Monograph treating hardness-based pseudorandomness in a unified theory.

notes: Priority ambiguity: Yao 1982 and Blum-Micali 1982 supply the hardness-to-pseudorandomness principle (cryptographic); Nisan-Wigderson 1988 supply the design-based, circuit-hardness version and the name. Dates for people (lifespan) are from general knowledge/Wikipedia, not independently verified here.

canonicalName: Measure rigidity of diagonal actions: Littlewood conjecture and arithmetic quantum unique ergodicity

evidence.claim: Furstenberg, Disjointness in ergodic theory, minimal sets, and a problem in diophantine approximation (1967): rigidity question for commuting maps (x2,x3) and orbit closures.

conceptual.note: Earliest public rigidity statement that I could evidence for diagonal/commuting actions. I did not read the 1967 text; its x2,x3 conjecture content and its link to Littlewood-type problems is from standard history, not checked. Littlewood conjecture itself is older (appears in Cassels-Swinnerton-Dyer 1955, Phil. Trans., 10.1098/rsta.1955.0010, which treats products of linear forms).

evidence.claim: Einsiedler, Katok, Lindenstrauss, Invariant measures and the set of exceptions to Littlewood conjecture, Annals 164 (2006).
Lindenstrauss, Invariant measures and arithmetic quantum unique ergodicity, Annals 163 (2006).

methodological.note: The two Annals papers perform the use of measure rigidity on the Littlewood problem and on QUE. Precursors: Rudolph 1990 (10.1017/s0143385700005629), Katok-Spatzier 1996 (10.1017/s0143385700009081); Rudnick-Sarnak 1994 posed QUE (10.1007/bf02099418).

evidence.claim: Annals paper titles naming Littlewood conjecture and arithmetic quantum unique ergodicity, 2006.
Textbook: Einsiedler-Ward, Ergodic Theory with a view towards Number Theory (GTM 259, 2011).

institutional.note: Earliest indexed title found: zbMATH search ti:Littlewood conjecture 1950-2006 returned the 2006 paper as the only dynamics one; 2000 Pollington-Velani "Littlewood conjecture" title is a metric Diophantine paper. Corpus: zbMATH Open and Crossref only; MSC/ICM not checked.

firstTermUse.source: https://zbmath.org/?q=an:0820.11040 (Jakobson, QUE for Eisenstein series; earliest title in zbMATH ti:quantum unique ergodicity 1990-2005)

works.citation: Furstenberg, Disjointness in ergodic theory, minimal sets, and a problem in diophantine approximation
works.whyItMatters: Origin of the rigidity question for x2,x3.

works.citation: Rudolph, x2 and x3 invariant measures and entropy
works.whyItMatters: First major positive-entropy rigidity theorem.

works.citation: Katok and Spatzier, Invariant measures for higher-rank hyperbolic abelian actions
works.whyItMatters: Entropy and rigidity for higher-rank abelian actions.

works.citation: Einsiedler, Katok, Lindenstrauss, Invariant measures and the set of exceptions to Littlewood conjecture
works.whyItMatters: Partial resolution of Littlewood conjecture.

works.citation: Lindenstrauss, Invariant measures and arithmetic quantum unique ergodicity
works.whyItMatters: Proved arithmetic QUE (non-escape of mass completed later by Soundararajan).

works.citation: Rudnick and Sarnak, The behaviour of eigenstates of arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds
works.whyItMatters: Formulated the QUE conjecture in the arithmetic setting.

notes: Event bundles two targets. Lindenstrauss 2006 plus later work (Soundararajan, Holowinsky) completed QUE for compact and noncompact cases; the catalogue summary says partial resolution, consistent with EKL (Hausdorff dimension zero of exceptions). Lifespans for Katok, Rudolph from general knowledge.

canonicalName: Old Babylonian algebra: quadratic and cubic problem solving

evidence.claim: MacTutor describes Old Babylonian tablets with rectangle-area problems leading to quadratic equations and a standard solving method.
Same page puts Babylonian rule from about 2000 BC and capital at Babylon by about 1900 BC.

conceptual.note: Ancient texts; no precise publication date. Range -2000 to -1600 is the Old Babylonian period as conventionally used; MacTutor dating of the period is approximate and I did not find an independent source for exact tablet dates. Modern first publication of the texts (the sense of "publicly published"): Neugebauer MKT 1935 and Thureau-Dangin 1938. Earlier Sumerian/Akkadian-era computation tables exist (MacTutor: tablets ~2000 BC).

evidence.claim: MacTutor: BM 85200+ holds 36 cellar-volume problems and is described as the earliest known attempt to set up and solve cubic problems of this type.

methodological.note: Application to excavation and area problems is attested in Old Babylonian tablets (YBC 4666, 7164, VAT 7528, BM 85196 per MacTutor). Individual tablet dates not evidenced by me; range is the period range.

evidence.claim: Gandz, The origin and development of the quadratic equations in Babylonian, Greek and early Arabic algebra (1937): earliest indexed title naming Babylonian quadratic equations.
Neugebauer, Mathematische Keilschrift-Texte, 1935: standard edition of the mathematical tablets.

institutional.note: Ancient scribal "curriculum" is institutional in antiquity but undated; this is the earliest modern titled study found in zbMATH (queries: ti:Babylonian algebra 1900-1960, ti:Babylonian quadratic equations). Earlier French/German titles (Thureau-Dangin, 1930s) not checked. Later: Hoyrup, Lengths, Widths, Surfaces (2002).

works.citation: Neugebauer, Mathematische Keilschrift-Texte
works.whyItMatters: Edition and translation that made the tablets available.

works.citation: Neugebauer and Sachs, Mathematical Cuneiform Texts
works.whyItMatters: English edition of key texts.

works.citation: Hoyrup, Lengths, Widths, Surfaces: A Portrait of Old Babylonian Algebra and Its Kin
works.whyItMatters: Geometrical-interpretation of the procedures; the main modern account.

works.citation: Robson, Mesopotamian Mathematics (in Mathematics of Egypt, Mesopotamia, China, India, and Islam)
works.whyItMatters: Modern synthesis of Mesopotamian mathematics.

works.citation: Gandz, The origin and development of the quadratic equations in Babylonian, Greek and early Arabic algebra
works.whyItMatters: Early study of the quadratic solution method.

notes: No named individual originator: anonymous scribes. Interpretive dispute: whether the procedures are "algebra" or geometry (Neugebauer algebraic reading vs Hoyrup geometrical reading, Unguru 1975 debate for Greek geometry). Cubic: MacTutor says tablets used n^3+n^2 tables. I could not verify actual tablet dates beyond the period. Lifespans from general knowledge.

canonicalName: Archimedean statics (On the Equilibrium of Planes; On Floating Bodies)

evidence.claim: MacTutor: On plane equilibriums sets out principles of mechanics using geometry methods; order of Archimedes writings uncertain; lifetime 287-212 BC.
Open Library: Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897), standard English edition.

conceptual.note: No evidenced date for the treatise; range is Archimedes lifetime. MacTutor says the chronological order is not known for certain (Heath vs Knorr 1978, 10.1007/bf00357582). Precursors not evidenced here: the pseudo-Aristotelian Mechanica and Archytas on mechanics are often cited; I did not search them.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Archimedes derived centres of gravity and treated mechanical theorems by geometrical proof.

methodological.note: Same range; Method (mechanical theorems used for area/volume) also by Archimedes, date unknown. Berggren 1976 (10.1007/bf00349632) examines spurious theorems in Equilibrium of Planes Book I.

evidence.claim: Stevin, De Beghinselen der Weeghconst (1586), Dutch treatise on statics (weeghconst).

institutional.note: Earliest dated treatise titled for statics that I evidenced; Archimedes own titles (On the Equilibrium of Planes, On Floating Bodies) are earlier but undated, and the medieval Jordanus/Liber de ponderibus tradition was not searched, so this is not claimed as first. Modern critical edition: Heiberg 1880-81 (Open Library OL15725084W).

works.citation: Archimedes, On the Equilibrium of Planes / On Floating Bodies (Heath ed., The Works of Archimedes)
works.whyItMatters: Source treatises; dated by edition, original date unknown.

works.citation: Stevin, De beghinselen der weeghconst
works.whyItMatters: Revived Archimedean statics; inclined plane law.

works.citation: Heiberg, Archimedis Opera omnia cum commentariis Eutocii
works.whyItMatters: Critical Greek text of the corpus.

works.citation: Heath, The Works of Archimedes
works.whyItMatters: English edition used for chronology cited by MacTutor.

works.citation: Dijksterhuis, Archimedes
works.whyItMatters: Modern monograph on the corpus (first Dutch edition 1938 per general knowledge, not verified).

notes: All three dates are essentially unknown for ancient works; only lifespan bounds evidenced. Type listed as fusion of geometry and mechanics: claim that this is the earliest such fusion is untested (Mechanica, Archytas). Lifespans for Heiberg, Stevin, Dijksterhuis from general knowledge.

canonicalName: Abstract (axiomatic) rings and fields; modern algebra

evidence.claim: Steinitz, Algebraische Theorie der Körper, Crelle 137 (1910).
MacTutor credits Steinitz with the first abstract definition of a field in that paper.
Fraenkel thesis On divisors of zero and decomposition of rings, Crelle 145: 1915 in Crossref; Jahrbuch/zbMATH lists 1914.

conceptual.note: Priority issue: Weber 1893 (Math. Ann. 43, 10.1007/bf01446451) gave abstract groups per MacTutor and is often credited with an axiomatic field definition too, but I did not obtain text evidence for the field axioms, so the 1910 date follows MacTutor. Dedekind introduced the term Körper for number fields (MacTutor Ring theory page) in 1871 (concrete, subfields of C); Hilbert coined Zahlring/ring (MacTutor), year not evidenced. Rings: Fraenkel 1914/1915 abstract ring paper; Noether 1921.

evidence.claim: Noether, Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen, Math. Ann. 83 (1921): ideal theory carried out for abstract rings.
MacTutor: Noether c. 1921 unified rings of polynomials and rings of numbers under one theory; axiomatic commutative ring theory developed in the 1920s.

methodological.note: First purposeful use of the abstract ring concept on a target problem (primary decomposition for ideals). Steinitz 1910 also applied the abstract field theory to transcendence degree and algebraic closures.

evidence.claim: Paper title naming the theory of fields: Algebraische Theorie der Körper (1910).
Textbook: van der Waerden, Moderne Algebra, Bd. I (1930), Bd. II (1931).

institutional.note: Earliest title found naming the field theory is Steinitz 1910; first textbook named Moderne Algebra is 1930 (later also Weber Lehrbuch der Algebra 1895-96, zbMATH 27.0056.01, not abstract in MacTutor view). If institutional means a textbook for the whole subject, use 1930.

works.citation: Weber, Die allgemeinen Grundlagen der Galois-schen Gleichungstheorie, Math. Ann. 43
works.whyItMatters: Abstract group (and likely field) framework; MacTutor stresses groups.

works.citation: Steinitz, Algebraische Theorie der Körper, Crelle 137
works.whyItMatters: First systematic abstract theory of fields.

works.citation: Fraenkel, Uber die Teiler der Null und die Zerlegung von Ringen, Crelle 145
works.whyItMatters: Abstract rings with zero divisors; Crossref 1915, JFM 1914.

works.citation: Noether, Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen, Math. Ann. 83
works.whyItMatters: Axiomatic ideal theory of rings.

works.citation: van der Waerden, Moderne Algebra Bd. I
works.whyItMatters: First textbook presentation built on rings and fields.

notes: Dedekind (Koerper 1871, ideals), Kronecker, Hilbert (Zahlbericht, ring) and Weber 1893/1895 are precursors; not all dated here because text evidence was lacking. Fraenkel year discrepancy: 1914 (zbMATH/JFM) vs 1915 (Crossref journal volume). Dedekind omitted from people because no bibliographic work record with year was obtained.

canonicalName: Arbuthnot's argument from the sex ratio (early significance test)

evidence.claim: Arbuthnot, An argument for divine providence, taken from the constant regularity observed in the births of both sexes, Phil. Trans. (record year 1710).

conceptual.note: Crossref record year is the volume year; the paper is often dated 1710/1711. Not verified: whether the first public print precedes 1711 (volume covers 1710-12). Private priority: Nicolaus Bernoulli wrote letters on the topic in 1712-13 (Shoesmith 1985, 10.2307/1402889; Ruiz-Garzon 2018 Zbl 1408.01004); these are later than Arbuthnot.

evidence.claim: Same paper performs the probability computation on London christenings records.
Bellhouse writes on Arbuthnot and chance; Shoesmith on the continental controversy over the argument.

methodological.note: The use of probability on demographic data is the paper itself. Graunt, Natural and Political Observations (1662; Open Library OL7013552W) predates it as statistical demography but without a probability test.

evidence.claim: Guillard, Elements de statistique humaine, ou demographie comparee (1855): book titled with the new term demography.

institutional.note: Earliest named textbook for the target field demography. For significance testing as a named subject: Pearson 1900 chi-square paper (10.1080/14786440009463897), Fisher Statistical Methods for Research Workers 1925 (Open Library OL1153861W); term not searched for earlier use.

works.citation: Arbuthnot, An argument for divine providence ... births of both sexes
works.whyItMatters: The test-like argument.

works.citation: Shoesmith, Nicholas Bernoulli and the argument for divine providence
works.whyItMatters: Secondary study of Bernoulli reply to Arbuthnot.

works.citation: de Moivre, The Doctrine of Chances
works.whyItMatters: Normal approximation later used on the sex-ratio problem (reprint record).

works.citation: Pearson, On the criterion that a given system of deviations ... random sampling
works.whyItMatters: Formal goodness-of-fit test.

works.citation: Fisher, Statistical Methods for Research Workers
works.whyItMatters: Popularised significance testing.

notes: Whether Arbuthnot is the first significance test is a historical claim (Stigler, Hacking) that I did not read; I only evidenced the paper. The 1718 de Moivre year is the first-edition year from general knowledge; Crossref link is a reprint. Lifespans from general knowledge.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Leray published papers introducing sheaves and the spectral sequence of a continuous map; MacTutor refs cite Miller on the Oflag XVIIA origins.
Leray 1946 Comptes rendus notes on the homology ring of a map (e.g. L anneau d homologie d une representation; Structure de l anneau ...).

conceptual.note: Year 1946 from the two zbMATH records; I did not read their content to confirm that sheaves (faisceaux) are introduced there rather than in Leray 1950 (J. Math. Pures Appl. 29). Leray did the work in captivity 1940-45 (MacTutor), published after liberation: the 1945 JMPA paper Sur la forme des espaces topologiques (Zbl 0060.40703) is an earlier candidate not checked for sheaves.

evidence.claim: Serre, Faisceaux algebriques coherents, Annals of Mathematics 61 (1955): sheaf cohomology applied to algebraic varieties.
Grothendieck, Sur quelques points d algebre homologique, Tohoku 1957.

methodological.note: First purposeful application to algebraic geometry. Earlier application to several complex variables (Cartan seminars 1948-1954, Oka-Cartan Cousin problems) per MacTutor, but no dated paper obtained for that.

evidence.claim: Paper title naming sheaves: Faisceaux algebriques coherents (1955).
Godement, Topologie algebrique et theorie des faisceaux (1958), first textbook on the subject.

institutional.note: Title search zbMATH ti:faisceaux 1946-1952 showed no sheaf-theory titles; Cartan seminar 1950-51 (MacTutor) was a sheaf-theory seminar but I did not evidence its title. Textbook date 1958 if a book is required.

evidence.claim: Iwasawa, On Gamma-extensions of algebraic number fields, Bull. AMS 65 (1959).
Iwasawa, On the theory of cyclotomic fields, Annals 70 (1959).

Iwasawa, On p-adic L-functions, Annals 89 (1969): linking p-adic L-functions to the Iwasawa module structure (main conjecture setting).

aliases: truth-functional logic with more than two values

evidence.claim: SEP: first explicit systems of many-valued logics were Lukasiewicz short note on three-valued logic (1920) and Post (1921).
evidence.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Many-Valued Logic

evidence.claim: Post, Introduction to a general theory of elementary propositions, Am. J. Math. 43 (1921).

conceptual.note: Lukasiewicz note appeared in Ruch Filozoficzny (1920); I found no bibliographic record of it (not in Crossref/zbMATH), so the year relies on SEP. Post 1921 in print, work from 1920 (earlier private/dissertation details not checked). Earlier challenges: MacColl 1906, Vasiliev, Peirce (SEP).

evidence.claim: Lukasiewicz, Philosophical remarks on many-valued systems of propositional logic (zbMATH 1931 record, JFM 57.1319.02).
SEP: systematic investigations began in the 1930s, spurred by axiomatising Lukasiewicz logic.

methodological.note: Purposeful application of many-valued logic to philosophical targets (future contingents, modality): Lukasiewicz 1920 note itself applied the third value to possibility (SEP); 1930 philosophical remarks. The first application to a mathematical target (e.g. Rosser-Turquette 1952 completeness) is later; choice of 1930 is weak.

evidence.claim: Title naming many-valued logics: Vaidyanathaswamy, Quasi-boolean algebras and many-valued logics (1938).
Lukasiewicz 1931 title with many-valued systems (earlier, JFM 57.1319.02).
Textbook: Rosser and Turquette, Many-valued logics (1952); Rescher, Many-valued logic (1969).

institutional.note: Earliest indexed title in zbMATH naming many-valued systems of logic: Lukasiewicz, Philosophical remarks on many-valued systems of propositional logic (zbMATH year 1931; original 1930 Comptes rendus Varsovie per general knowledge, not verified). First title with the exact phrase "many-valued logics": Vaidyanathaswamy 1938; textbook Rosser-Turquette 1952. Corpus: zbMATH only.

works.citation: Lukasiewicz, Philosophical remarks on many-valued systems of propositional logic
works.whyItMatters: Developed the three- and n-valued systems philosophically.

works.citation: Post, Introduction to a general theory of elementary propositions
works.whyItMatters: Defined n-valued propositional calculi and functional completeness.

works.citation: Rosser and Turquette, Many-valued logics
works.whyItMatters: First textbook on the subject.

works.citation: Rescher, Many-valued logic
works.whyItMatters: Standard textbook.

notes: Priority: Lukasiewicz (1920, three-valued, motivated by future contingents) and Post (1921, n-valued, functional completeness) are independent; Post probably had results in 1920. SEP lists earlier precursors (MacColl 1906, Peirce, Vasiliev) not rated here as systems. Lifespans from general knowledge.
